question: Why does the rule "Make argument order unambiguous at the call site" matter in a code review?

expected_rule_sections.heading: Make argument order unambiguous at the call site
heading_path: Clean Code, Chapter 8: Function Heuristics, PR review rules
Make argument order unambiguous at the call site

relevant_concepts: Make argument order unambiguous at the call site

Every argument makes a function harder to understand. Zero or one is easiest, two is manageable because there is only one way to get the order wrong, three has five wrong orders, and four has twenty-three. Arguments are harder to read than to write, because the IDE helps while writing but much less while reading. Three is a usual limit, though an arbitrary one. Keyword arguments relieve most of the order worry.

question: What review guidance applies to "Avoid output arguments"?

expected_rule_sections.heading: Avoid output arguments
heading_path: Clean Code, Chapter 8: Function Heuristics, PR review rules
Avoid output arguments

relevant_concepts: Readers expect data to go in through arguments and come out through the return value. Output arguments violate the principle of least surprise and force a double take. Where objects exist, the object itself can hold the results.

question: Why does the rule "Separate commands from queries" matter in a code review?

expected_rule_sections.heading: Separate commands from queries
heading_path: Clean Code, Chapter 8: Function Heuristics, PR review rules
Separate commands from queries

relevant_concepts: A function should either do something (a command that changes state) or answer something (a query), not both. `if set(...)` could mean "was it already set?" or "was it successfully set?", because `set` reads like an adjective instead of a verb. Even convenient violations have costs: without atomicity, `pop` can race and hand one item to two threads, and returning a value while altering state can leave a container in an unknown state if an exception occurs.
